explanation_en: The balance of payments (BOP) includes the current account, capital account, and financial account. The net balance of all entries in a country's BOP accounts should theoretically always equal zero. A deficit in one or two of the components must be offset by an equivalent surplus in the other(s). Since initially there is a deficit in the current and financial accounts, the capital account must be in surplus. Appreciation of a country's currency reduces the cost of imports and increases the cost of exports and, as a result, adversely affects the country's trade balance (ie, current account). Given no change in the financial account deficit, an increase in the current account deficit must be counterbalanced by an equal increase in the capital account surplus (Choices A and C).

question_en: A country has deficits in both its current account and financial account. Its currency appreciates significantly, causing the current account deficit to increase. Assuming no change in the financial account, which of the following must occur to keep the balance of payments in balance?
explanation_en: Identifying the buy side or the sell side in a currency trade may seem arbitrary since every trade entails a purchase and sale of different currencies by both trade counterparties. The foreign exchange (FX) market follows the conventions of other financial markets and designates the intermediaries as the sell side. The sell side is composed of the banks that trade currencies and provide related products. Due to economies of scale a preponderance of trading occurs at a handful of global money center banks (ie, first-tier banks). In addition to being market makers these banks sell currencies and provide related products (eg, currency derivatives, trade financing) to their clients. Although not major currency market players, regional and local banks (ie, second- and third-tier banks) provide similar currency-related products to their customers. (Choice B) Corporations other than banks are part of the buy side of the currency market. (Choice C) Central banks are part of the buy side of the currency market.

question_en:
An analyst gathers the following information:

|   |   |
|---|---|
| Spot CAD/AUD | 0.9434 |
| AUD Consumer Price Index | 119.7 |
| Expected Australian inflation rate | 2.0% |
| CAD Consumer Price Index | 144.4 |
| Expected Canadian inflation rate | 3.50% |

The real CAD/AUD exchange rate is closest to:
explanation_en:
Real exchange rate (Domestic/Foreign) = Nominal exchange rate (Domestic/Foreign) x (Price level Foreign / Price level Domestic).

Real exchange rates are used to measure the relative purchasing power between two currencies. Relative purchasing power is measured by adjusting the nominal exchange rate by the ratio of the aggregate price levels for similar goods in each currency.

Based on the formula shown above, the real exchange rate:
- varies directly with the nominal exchange rate and the foreign price level, and
- varies inversely with the domestic price level (which itself is typically measured using a consumer price index).

In this case, CAD is the domestic currency and AUD is the foreign currency:

Real exchange rate (CAD/AUD) = 0.9434 x (119.7 / 144.4) = 0.7820

If the purchasing power of both currencies were the same, the real exchange rate would equal 1.0 and the nominal exchange rate would need to be adjusted to offset the relative price level difference (ie, the nominal exchange rate would be the inverse of the ratio of price levels).

As the real exchange rate rises (falls), the relative purchasing power of the domestic currency declines (increases), such that imported foreign goods become more expensive (cheaper). If the real exchange rate falls below zero (as in this case), the domestic currency's relative purchasing power has increased (ie, imported foreign-priced goods become more affordable).

(Choice B) 0.9575 results from using the relative inflation rate, instead of price levels, to adjust the nominal exchange rate.

(Choice C) 1.1380 results from mistakenly inverting the ratio of foreign to domestic price levels.

Things to remember: Real exchange rates measure the relative purchasing power between two currencies. To calculate a real exchange rate, adjust the spot exchange rate by the ratio of foreign to domestic price levels (measured by the two currencies' consumer price indexes).

An exchange quote in either currency is the reciprocal of the other: CHF/EUR = 1/(CHF/EUR = EUR/CHF). This remains true even as exchange rates move. Consequently, 1 + percentage changes in the two currencies are inversely proportional. Given a percentage change in either the base or price currency, the percentage change in the other can always be calculated. Insert the percentage appreciation in CHF on the right-hand side of the equation and solve for the percentage depreciation in EUR. (Choice B) 4.00% is the percentage appreciation of CHF. The percentage decline in the depreciating currency is always smaller than the percentage increase in the appreciating currency. question_en: If a Brazilian converts BRL 781.25 to EUR 125, then the direct exchange rate from the Brazilian's perspective is closest to:
explanation_en: The balance of payments (BOP) summarizes a country's international capital inflows and outflows. BOP accounting is based on a double-entry bookkeeping system. All transactions are allocated to either the current account, the capital account, or the financial account. Broadly speaking, the current account reflects the net value of imported and exported goods and services but can be further subdivided into: Merchandise trade: Import and export of physical commodities and manufactured goods Services: Service industry imports and exports (eg, software, movies, legal services) Income receipts: Income from foreign assets, such as dividend income or interest payments Unilateral transfers: One-way transfers, such as foreign aid or worker remittance In each account, debits increase assets or decrease liabilities whereas credits decrease assets or increase liabilities. In this instance, a US investor receiving a dividend payment from a French company (which is an income receipt in the US) results in a debit (ie, increase in assets) to the US current account. (Choice B) The financial account captures cross-border transfers of assets, not the income or interest received from owning an asset. (Choice C) The capital account captures sales and transfers of nonproduced and intangible assets, such as mineral rights or patents.

explanation_en: Government policies to place limits on foreign markets Quotas Tariffs Trade restrictions Voluntary export restraints (limits on goods) Export subsidies Domestic content provisions Capital restrictions Restrictions on inflows from foreigners (limits on capital) Restrictions on outflows by citizens Capital restrictions are used by governments and other regulatory bodies to limit a country's openness to foreign markets. Unlike trade restrictions, which limit the flow of international goods, capital restrictions limit the flow of capital to and from international sources. Capital restrictions can limit foreigners' ability to own domestic assets and can limit citizens' ability to own foreign assets. Restrictions on inflows include limiting how much foreigners can invest in an asset (eg, real estate) and imposing maximum levels on foreign ownership in strategic industries (eg, defense). Restrictions on outflows include capping the amount domestic citizens can invest abroad and imposing deadlines for repatriation of foreign capital and investments. (Choice A) Capital restrictions set conditions on the flow of capital to and from other countries and are not used to reduce imports of a good. Trade restrictions are policies that set conditions on trade with other countries. (Choice C) Capital restrictions may be imposed to restrict flight of foreign capital in times of macroeconomic crisis, when a rapid recall of foreign funds could leave domestic companies more vulnerable. During times of economic expansion, the risk of a rapid recall of foreign funds is lower, so capital restrictions are unlikely to be needed.

question_en: An analyst gathers the following information related to the New Zealand dollar (NZD) and the Australian dollar (AUD): Based on this information, the maximum arbitrage profits (in AUD) are closest to:
explanation_en: When the risk-free interest rates of two countries are different, the forward rates of their currencies must be priced to prevent arbitrage profit in an efficient market. The forward rate calculation is based on the spot rate, the interest rates, and the length of the forward period. In this scenario, since a dealer is offering a rate of 1.1700 NZD/AUD, which differs from the arbitrage-free rate, arbitrage profits are possible. According to the arbitrage-free rate, AUD 1.000 should purchase NZD 1.1974. However, using the dealer quote, AUD 1.000 only purchases NZD 1.1700. Therefore, in the market, the AUD is underpriced and the NZD is overpriced. Arbitrage profits can be earned by committing today to sell (ie, deliver) the overpriced NZD and to buy (ie, take delivery of) the underpriced AUD through a forward exchange rate contract. One of the key elements of arbitrage is that investors do not risk their own funds, but instead borrow to initiate the transaction. In this scenario, the first step is to borrow AUD to obtain the NZD, which will be invested and eventually delivered under the forward contract. The complete steps to exploit this opportunity are as follows: (Choice A) 0.0120 represents the difference between the arbitrage-free forward exchange rate and the market rate, or 1/1.1700 − 1/1.1974 (quotes are inverted to obtain the AUD result). (Choice C) 0.0276 represents the loss that would be incurred by entering into a forward contract to sell the AUD (ie, underpriced asset) and buy the NZD (ie, overpriced asset). This transaction is unlikely since it would lock in a loss.

question_en: A GBP/USD forward exchange rate quoted at positive forward points most likely indicates that GBP:
option_a: is expected to appreciate against USD.
option_b: is trading at a forward discount relative to USD.
option_c: has an interest rate that is lower than the USD interest rate.
explanation_en: A forward exchange rate is the amount of one currency that can be exchanged for one unit of another currency in the future; this rate can be quoted by forward points. The forward exchange rate is determined by adding the quoted number of positive or negative forward points, also known as pips, to the price currency in the spot rate quote. If there are: Positive forward points, then the specified number of pips is added to the spot rate to determine the forward exchange rate. In this scenario, it takes more GBP (ie, price currency) to buy USD 1 at the forward rate than at the spot rate. This means each GBP is worth less relative to the USD in the forward market, so the GBP is trading at a forward discount. Negative forward points, then the specified number of pips is subtracted from the spot rate to determine the forward exchange rate. In that case, it takes fewer GBP to buy USD 1 at the forward rate than at the spot rate. This means each GBP is worth more relative to the USD in the forward market, so the GBP is trading at a forward premium. (Choice A) The positive points signal that it will take a greater amount of GBP to buy USD 1 at the forward rate than at the spot rate and that market participants expect the GBP to depreciate against the USD. (Choice C) A forward exchange rate greater than the spot rate indicates that the price currency interest rate is greater than the base currency interest rate.

question_en: A currency trader observes the following currency spot exchange rates from two dealers: Based on only this information, the arbitrage profit available per every CNY 1 is closest to:
explanation_en: A cross-rate is the exchange rate implied by two related exchange rates, assuming that no arbitrage opportunities exist. If the actual exchange rate differs from the no-arbitrage exchange rate implied by the cross-rate, then an arbitrage opportunity exists. An investor can profit by purchasing a currency from the source where it is underpriced and simultaneously selling the same currency to the source where it is overpriced. Finding an arbitrage opportunity from cross-rates can be conceptualized as a triangle, as shown above. Potential arbitrage profits can be observed by moving from one currency to another in two directions around the triangle. When moving around the triangle, one currency is multiplied by the actual exchange rate to convert to another currency. In this scenario, the INR/CNY rate from Dealer 2 is 10.75. Using the INR/THB and CNY/THB rates quoted by Dealer 1, Dealer 1's INR/CNY cross- rate is 10.6818. The arbitrage profit is the difference between buying CNY 1 for INR 10.6818 from Dealer 1 and simultaneously selling CNY 1 for INR 10.75 to Dealer 2. The profit is INR 10.75 − INR 10.6818 = INR 0.0682 per every CNY 1 (Choice C). (Choice B) 0.0064 is the potential arbitrage profit in CNY, not INR.

question_en: The EUR/GBP spot exchange rate is 1.1650. The EUR one-year interest rate is 0.25%, and the GBP one-year interest rate is 1.50%. The one- year forward exchange rate expressed in forward points is closest to:
explanation_en: Exchange rate quotes specify the amount of one currency to be traded for one unit of another currency. The value is expressed in units of the price currency per one unit of the base currency. If the EUR/GBP exchange rate is quoted at 1.1650, it costs 1.1650 EUR (the price currency) to purchase one GBP (the base currency). The spot exchange rate is the value at which one currency can be traded for another today. The forward exchange rate is the current quotation for the value at which one currency can be exchanged for another in the future. The difference between the spot and forward exchange rates is determined by the relative level of risk-free interest rates in the two currencies. Given the spot rate and one-year interest rates in the two currencies, the one-year forward rate can be calculated. The forward points equal forward exchange rate minus the spot exchange rate, with the difference multiplied by 10,000 (unless the JPY is one of the currency pair, in which case the multiplier is 100). (Choice B) −115 is the negative of the one-year forward exchange rate. (Choice C) 145 is the result if the EUR and GBP interest rates are inverted in the forward exchange rate calculation.

question_en: The USD/GBP spot rate is 1.3075, and the one-year USD/GBP forward rate is 1.3266. If the one-year USD risk-free interest rate is 4.00%, then the one-year GBP risk-free interest rate is closest to:
explanation_en: When the risk-free interest rates for two countries differ, the forward exchange rate between their currencies will differ from the spot (ie, current) exchange rate. A foreign exchange quote specifies the amount of price currency that can be acquired for each unit of base currency. When the forward rate is: less than the spot rate, the price currency is trading at a forward premium to the base currency. greater than the spot rate, the price currency is trading at a forward discount to the base currency. A forward premium signals that market participants expect the price currency to appreciate relative to the base currency: in the future, one unit of base currency will buy less price currency than it does today since the price currency has become more valuable than the base currency. A forward discount signals that the price currency is expected to depreciate relative to the base currency. (Choice A) When the price currency is trading at a forward premium, the forward rate is less than the spot rate and the forward points are negative. (Choice C) When the price currency is trading at a forward premium, its interest rate must be less than the base currency's interest rate. The currency with the lower interest rate trades at a forward premium.
